title: Runbook authoring and maintenance guidelines
author: Priya Shah
content:
Summary:
This document defines standardized conventions, minimum content, and maintenance cadence for runbooks used by Platform Operators at Redwood Inference. It is intended for authors (SREs, Platform Engineers, Operators) who create or update runbooks that are used during oncall, incident response, and routine maintenance.

Goals:
- Ensure runbooks are actionable in the first 5 minutes of an incident.
- Make ownership, escalation, and rollback steps explicit.
- Reduce cognitive load for oncall engineers by standardizing format and signal-to-action mappings.

When to write a runbook:
1) New operational procedure that must be executed by oncall (eg. graceful cache shard rebalance).
2) A recurring incident pattern with a documented fast-path mitigation.
3) Any manual play that is part of a scheduled maintenance or emergency operation.

Runbook minimum schema (required sections):
1. Title and short summary (1 sentence)
2. Service(s) / components covered (explicit service names and team ownership)
3. Severity and WHEN to use this runbook (SLO triggers / alerts)
4. Preconditions / safety checks (what must be true before you start)
5. Step-by-step mitigation (numbered) with exact CLI/API commands
6. Rollback / undo steps
7. Post-incident validation (observability checks, dashboards to inspect)
8. Estimated RTO / RPO and expected impact during mitigation
9. Owner and reviewer (with oncall rotation alignment)
10. Change history and test notes

Authoring conventions (style & content):
- Keep the first actionable step visible above the fold. The doc should surface the 2–3 commands an operator needs immediately.
- Use explicit commands (not "run the deploy script") with a code block including arguments. When secrets/KMS keys are required, reference the secret by path (e.g., secrets/kms/ops-tool) but do not include values.
- Use the active voice and imperative form for steps (e.g., "Run: curl -X POST ...").
- Annotate each step with: expected duration, blast radius (low/medium/high), and safety checks.
- Prefer idempotent operations where possible and explain when an operation is non-idempotent.

Template (copy into a new runbook):
---
Title: <short-summary>
Service: <service-name> (team: <team-name>)
When to run: <alert-name / SLO threshold / metric condition>
Impact: <user-facing impact description>
Preconditions:
- <check 1>
- <check 2>
Primary run steps:
1) Step description
   - Command: ```bash
     <command with flags>
     ```
   - Expected time: 30s-2m
   - Blast radius: medium
   - Safety checks: <eg. check healthy replicas > 2>
2) Verification: 
   - Query: ```bash
     curl -s "https://metrics/api?query=up{service=\"<service-name>\"}"
     ```
Rollback steps:
- Step A: description and command
Post-incident tasks:
- Notify: channel #platform-incident and tag owner
- Run smoke tests: <link to smoke suite>
Changelog:
- 2026-01-12: Minor wording updates (Priya Shah)
---

Observability mappings (what to include in the runbook):
- Primary alert name and runbook link (alert rule metadata must include runbook link)
- 3 quick queries for triage (latency, error-rate, token-cost), with example PromQL/Flux/SQL
- Dashboard panels to check (provide direct panel URLs when possible)
- Synthetic checks to run after mitigation (example curl or synthetic ID)

Example observability snippet (Prometheus style):
- High error rate triage:
  promql: 'sum(rate(http_requests_total{job=\"platform-proxy\",status=~\"5..\"}[1m])) by (instance) > 10'
  quick-check: 'curl -sS https://platform-proxy.internal/health || true'

Ownership, review and lifecycle:
- Primary owner: the team responsible for the service (not the person oncall). Use the team alias in the owner field (eg. infra-platform).
- Reviewer: at least one cross-team reviewer when the runbook action could affect multiple services (eg. network, tenant-slice).
- Review cadence: quarterly automated reminders for runbooks that are tagged with the label 'oncall-critical'.
- Review required when: alerting thresholds change, SLOs are updated, or the service release includes behavioral changes to request handling.

Change control and versioning:
- Small edits (typo/clarity) can be merged to the runbook with a reviewer approval. Record change in the Changelog section.
- Major changes (new destructive steps, changes to safety checks) require a review from 2 approvers including an SRE and a Platform Owner. Mark the runbook as 'in_review' until approved.
- Runbooks are treated as code: store critical runbooks in the infra-docs repo as markdown with a link to the Confluence page and include CI validation (see CI checks below).

CI validation checklist (examples to include in repo CI):
- Linting: ensure required sections exist and header formats match the template.
- Link checking: verify referenced dashboard/panel URLs respond 200.
- Command safety scan: basic static checks to flag non-idempotent shell constructs (eg. unchecked 'rm -rf').
- Secret detection: fail on inline secrets or credentials.

Maintenance cadence and automation:
- Weekly: oncall engineers may flag out-of-date runbooks in the #runbook-maintenance channel.
- Monthly: runbook owners receive automated emails for runbooks with > 6 months since last validation.
- Quarterly: 'oncall-critical' runbooks must be exercise-tested in a tabletop or live-gameday. Record test results in the runbook's Change history.
- Yearly: archive runbooks that have not been exercised and have no active alerts referencing them.

How to exercise a runbook (tabletop / canary test):
1) Author and owner coordinate a 30–60 minute tabletop with at least two operators present.
2) Walk through steps aloud and confirm commands produce the expected checks.
3) If safe, perform the primary verification steps in a staging environment and capture logs/screenshots.
4) Record results and update the Changelog and last_validated date.

Incident-to-runbook flow (practical):
- Alert fires -> Oncall pulls runbook -> Triage (3 quick queries) -> Execute mitigation steps 1..N -> Verify -> Escalate if not resolved -> Run rollback if required -> Post-incident tasks.

Example: "kv-prefix-cache partial degradation" runbook highlights:
- When to run: 'kv_prefix_cache_high_load' alert sustained > 3 min and p99 latency > 250ms
- First step (visible top): Query shard health and redirect traffic to warm shards
- Safety check: ensure eviction backlog < 1000 before redirecting writes
- Rollback: re-enable routing weights to original values and monitor p50/p99 for 10m

Appendix A — Recommended table of metadata (copy into top of runbook):
| field | example | notes |
|-------|---------|-------|
| title | kv-prefix-cache partial degradation | short and action oriented |
| service | kv-prefix-cache | canonical service name |
| owner | infra-platform | team alias |
| severity | P1 | mapping to incident response process |
| runbook_link | /confluence/... | add to alert metadata |

Appendix B — Quick maintenance checklist (to paste into PR descriptions):
- [ ] Confirm owner & reviewer fields are current
- [ ] Validate all commands in a staging sandbox or annotate as untested
- [ ] Confirm linked dashboards resolve and show expected signals
- [ ] Add test notes to Change history

FAQs:
Q: Who can mark a runbook as deprecated?
A: The service owner or Platform Oncall Lead. Deprecation requires publishing a replacement or confirmation there is no active alert referencing the runbook.

Q: Can runbooks include scripts?
A: Prefer inline commands in the runbook and reference scripts in a versioned repo. If including scripts, include exact repo tag/commit and CI badge.

Appendix C — Useful links and templates:
- Runbook template (markdown): https://repo.internal/infra-docs/runbook-template.md
- Runbook CI checks: https://ci.internal/pipelines/runbook-lint
- Oncall rotation calendar: https://calendar.internal/platform-oncall
